versions.problem: In MVFA's few-shot inference, the released code min-max normalises the zero-shot (text) branch and the few-shot (memory-bank) branch with the minimum and maximum over the entire test set and adds them with a fixed weight of 0.5; the image score is then the maximum of the fused pixel map. The score of one image, and therefore the reported AUROC, depends on which other images are in the test set, and the scorer cannot be applied to a single incoming image. Can this transductive normalisation be replaced by an inductive, per-image one that normalises each branch with statistics computed only from the K normal support images (leave-one-out scores of each support against the remaining supports' memory bank and against the text anchors), keeping the fusion weight and the max pooling unchanged, and at what cost in image-level and pixel-level AUROC? Outcomes per held-out BMAD dataset and K in {2, 4, 8, 16}: (i) the spread of the original method's AUROC across random test subsets and at shifted prevalence (10% and 50% abnormal), (ii) image- and pixel-level AUROC of inductive versus transductive normalisation, and (iii) sensitivity at 95% specificity and expected calibration error at a threshold fixed from the support scores alone.
versions.rationale: The code check turned L10 into a sharper limitation (C1): the fusion is computed with test-set extremes, which makes the method non-deployable on a stream of images and makes its numbers depend on test-set composition; L8 adds that only threshold-free AUROC is reported, so this dependence is invisible. Related work changes representations, prompts and fusion layers (LaRP-CLIP's adaptive fusion [57], HeadCLIP's joint score [17], ClipMPCAD [62]) but evaluates with the same AUROC; QueCo [56] goes further and builds its reference from the unlabelled test set itself, while CANOR [30] shows that a handful of calibration scalars can be learnt cheaply for a frozen CLIP. MVFA already loads K normal support images per modality but never uses them for normalisation, so an inductive normaliser needs no new data and no retraining: the change is confined to the scoring code (test_few.py) and runs on the released checkpoints retrained under the shared protocol. Keeping the pooling fixed isolates one component; the pooling question (L38, C3) can then be studied separately on top of a per-image score.

Clarity.review: The defect (test-set min-max normalisation before the 0.5 fusion) and the inductive replacement are precisely described, pooling and fusion weight are explicitly held fixed, and the outcomes are concrete. Three outcomes are bundled, however, and the leave-one-out statistic is ambiguous: it is not said whether min and max, or robust quantiles, of the support scores are used.
Clarity.feedback: Make the inductive normaliser the primary question and the test-set dependence analysis its motivating measurement; specify the statistic (e.g., mean and standard deviation, or the 1st and 99th percentiles, of leave-one-out support scores).

Relevance.review: Highly relevant: the code check (C1, L10) shows that MVFA's reported few-shot AUROCs depend on test-set extremes and that the method cannot score single images, which matters for both the validity of the published comparison and deployment.
Relevance.feedback: Mention whether the zero-shot evaluation script uses the same normalisation, which would extend relevance to the zero-shot tables.

Originality.review: Quantifying how a reported AUROC depends on transductive normalisation is uncommon in the CLIP anomaly-detection literature, and using the support set as the reference is a sensible, simple design. Calibration from normal references is, however, standard in classical anomaly detection, so the method itself is not new.
Originality.feedback: Position the work as an evaluation-validity study with a simple inductive fix rather than as a new fusion method.

Feasibility.review: Inference-only on retrained checkpoints, confined to test_few.py, with low compute. The weak point is K = 2: leave-one-out scores give two values per branch, so min-max statistics are degenerate and percentiles undefined.
Feasibility.feedback: Use pixel-level leave-one-out scores (all patches of the supports) rather than image-level ones, which gives thousands of values even at K = 2.

Significance.review: A per-image score with a threshold fixed from support images is the deployment property that AUROC hides; showing how much the published numbers depend on test-set composition would also change how future CLIP-based methods are evaluated on BMAD.
Significance.feedback: Report results so that other methods can adopt the inductive normaliser as an evaluation standard.

versions.problem: In MVFA's few-shot inference, the released code min-max normalises the zero-shot (text) branch and the few-shot (memory-bank) branch with the minimum and maximum over the entire test set and adds them with a fixed weight of 0.5, so the score of one image depends on the rest of the test set and a single incoming image cannot be scored. The inductive normaliser maps each branch's patch scores through the 1st and 99th percentiles of the leave-one-out patch scores of the supports (every patch of support i scored against the memory bank of the other K-1 supports and against the text anchors), which gives thousands of reference values even at K = 2; the fusion weight and the max pooling of the image score are kept fixed. Primary outcome: image-level and pixel-level AUROC of inductive versus transductive normalisation on each held-out BMAD dataset for K in {2, 4, 8, 16}. Motivating measurement: the spread of the original method's AUROC across random half-size test subsets and at shifted prevalence (10% and 50% abnormal). Secondary outcome: sensitivity at 95% specificity with a threshold fixed from the support scores alone.
versions.rationale: The code check turned L10 into a sharper limitation (C1): the fusion is computed with test-set extremes, which makes the method non-deployable on a stream of images and makes its numbers depend on test-set composition; L8 adds that only threshold-free AUROC is reported, so this dependence stays invisible. Related work changes representations, prompts and fusion layers (LaRP-CLIP [57], HeadCLIP [17], ClipMPCAD [62]) but evaluates with the same AUROC; QueCo [56] even builds its reference from the unlabelled test set, while CANOR [30] shows that a few calibration scalars can be fitted cheaply for a frozen CLIP. The study is positioned as an evaluation-validity study with a simple inductive fix: it reuses the K normal supports MVFA already loads, needs no retraining, is confined to test_few.py, and runs on checkpoints retrained under the shared protocol. Keeping the pooling fixed isolates one component, and the inductive normaliser can be adopted by other methods evaluated on BMAD.

Clarity.review: Primary, motivating and secondary outcomes are now separated, the leave-one-out statistic is defined (1st/99th percentiles of patch scores), and the fixed parts (fusion weight, max pooling) are explicit. The problem is precise and readable.

Relevance.review: High: it addresses the verified test-set dependence of MVFA's scores (C1, L10) and the missing operating-point evaluation (L8).

Originality.review: Framed as an evaluation-validity study with an inductive fix, it targets a practice the CLIP anomaly-detection literature has not examined ([17], [56], [57]); the fix itself (normalising by reference statistics) is standard.
Originality.feedback: Show whether other BMAD baselines share the transductive normalisation; that would make the finding broader than MVFA.

Feasibility.review: Inference-only, confined to one script; the patch-level leave-one-out statistic resolves the K = 2 problem. Compute is minimal.

Significance.review: A per-image score with a support-fixed threshold is a prerequisite for deployment, and quantifying the test-set dependence affects how published BMAD numbers are read.

versions.problem: In MVFA's zero-shot (leave-one-modality-out) training, only the segmentation adapters produce the anomaly maps, and the released code trains them with Dice and Focal losses exclusively on the three source datasets that have pixel masks (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC); the image-labelled datasets (OCT17, ChestXray, HIS) only train the detection adapters. Can the segmentation adapters be trained from image-level labels alone — replacing the Dice and Focal terms with a multiple-instance objective on each level's patch-to-text anomaly map (an image-level BCE on the top-k mean of patch anomaly probabilities, k = 1% of patches, so that an abnormal image must contain a few strongly abnormal patches and a normal image none) applied to all five source datasets with every mask discarded — and how much of the mask-supervised localisation (pixel-level AUROC and AUPRO) and detection (image-level AUROC) on the held-out modality does it retain? The comparison is mask-supervised MVFA versus image-label-supervised MVFA, trained and model-selected under the shared protocol.
versions.rationale: Limitations L3, L5 and L18, checked against the released code, show that MVFA's localisation depends on dense expert masks from three datasets and that half of the benchmark never teaches the segmentation branch anything; L4 shows the same dependence in the few-shot mode (K abnormal images with masks). Image-level labels are cheap and exist for every BMAD dataset, but MVFA never uses them to supervise where anomalies are. The related literature does not answer whether text-anchored patch similarities inside a multi-level CLIP adapter can learn localisation from weak labels: MedSAD-CLIP [40] and MLCA [58] keep pixel-level supervision, MadCLIP [29] and the consistency-margin adapter [54] still rely on labelled abnormal images, MediCLIP [22], AnomaMed [53] and the UWF framework [43] replace real labels with synthetic anomalies, and weak image-level supervision has been used for separate generative models (diffusion with classifier guidance [10]) rather than for the adapter's own maps. The question changes only the training signal of one branch, is implemented by replacing the segmentation loss in the public training script, and runs within one GPU budget; a negative result still quantifies what masks are worth for cross-modality localisation, which is exactly the annotation cost that L18 says is never measured.

Clarity.review: The component (segmentation adapters and their Dice/Focal loss), the change (an image-level BCE on the top-k mean of each level's patch anomaly probabilities, k = 1%, all five source datasets, masks discarded), the comparison and the outcomes are all named. Two details are left open: whether the MIL term is applied at all four adapter levels with equal weight, and whether the detection adapters keep their original loss unchanged.
Clarity.feedback: State that the MIL loss replaces the segmentation loss at every level with the same weights as the original, and that the detection branch is untouched; say that pixel-level metrics can only be computed on the held-out folds that have masks (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC).

Relevance.review: Mask dependence of MVFA's localisation is one of its most consequential limitations for clinical use, and the code-verified fact that half the benchmark never trains the segmentation branch (L5) makes the problem concrete. It connects to the annotation-efficiency concerns of [22], [40], [43] and [53].
Relevance.feedback: None of substance; briefly relate the result to the few-shot setting (L4, L18), where the same mask dependence appears.

Originality.review: Weakly supervised localisation through multiple-instance pooling is an established idea, and MVFA already applies a mean-pooled image-level BCE to its detection branch. The new element is narrower: supervising the text-anchored segmentation maps with image labels and testing whether the resulting localisation transfers to an unseen modality. This is a moderately original combination rather than a new idea.
Originality.feedback: Make the distinctive hypothesis explicit — for example, that text-anchored patch similarities let MIL localisation transfer across modalities, or that it emerges only at specific adapter levels — and test it with a level-wise analysis.

Feasibility.review: The change is one loss term in the public training script; BMAD provides image labels for every dataset; compute equals MVFA's own training. Two risks: MIL objectives can collapse to near-constant maps when abnormal images dominate a source dataset, and pixel-level evaluation is possible on only three of the held-out folds.
Feasibility.feedback: Run a single-fold pilot first and monitor the fraction of patches above 0.5 on normal validation images to detect collapse; report pixel metrics only where masks exist.

Significance.review: If localisation can be learnt without masks, MVFA-style adaptation becomes trainable from report-level labels, a substantial practical gain; a negative result still quantifies what masks are worth for cross-modality localisation, which the target paper never measures.
Significance.feedback: Add a label-budget view (many image-labelled images versus a few masked ones) so the result informs an annotation decision.

versions.problem: In MVFA's zero-shot (leave-one-modality-out) training, the segmentation adapters — the only part that produces anomaly maps — are trained with Dice and Focal losses exclusively on the three source datasets that have pixel masks (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC), while OCT17, ChestXray and HIS only train the detection adapters. Can the segmentation adapters be trained from image-level labels alone? At every one of the four adapter levels, with the original level weights, the Dice and Focal terms are replaced by an image-level BCE on the top-k mean of the level's patch anomaly probabilities (k = 1% of patches: an abnormal image must contain a few strongly abnormal patches, a normal image none), applied to all five source datasets with every mask discarded; the detection adapters and their loss are unchanged. Hypothesis: because the patch scores are similarities to fixed text anchors shared across modalities, this weak supervision yields localisation that transfers to the unseen modality, and it emerges mainly at the deeper adapter levels. Outcomes on the held-out modality: pixel-level AUROC and AUPRO (on the folds with masks: BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC), image-level AUROC (all folds), and a level-wise breakdown, comparing mask-supervised MVFA with image-label-supervised MVFA trained and model-selected under the shared protocol; a label-budget curve adds variants with masks for only 10% and 25% of the abnormal source images.
versions.rationale: Limitations L3, L5 and L18, checked against the released code, show that MVFA's localisation depends on dense expert masks from three datasets and that half of the benchmark never teaches the segmentation branch anything; L4 shows the same dependence in the few-shot mode. Image-level labels are cheap and available for every BMAD dataset, yet MVFA never uses them to supervise where anomalies are. The related literature does not answer whether text-anchored patch similarities inside a multi-level CLIP adapter can learn transferable localisation from weak labels: MedSAD-CLIP [40] and MLCA [58] keep pixel-level supervision, MadCLIP [29] and the consistency-margin adapter [54] rely on labelled abnormal images, MediCLIP [22], AnomaMed [53] and the UWF framework [43] replace labels with synthetic anomalies, and image-level supervision has been used for separate generative models [10] rather than for the adapter's own maps. The change is one loss term in the public training script at the original compute budget; a one-fold pilot that monitors the fraction of normal-image patches above 0.5 guards against collapsed maps. Either outcome is informative: success makes MVFA trainable from report-level labels, and failure, together with the label-budget curve, quantifies what masks are worth for cross-modality localisation — the cost that L18 says is never measured.

Clarity.review: The revision fixes the open details (all four levels, original weights, detection branch unchanged, pixel metrics only on masked folds) and states a testable hypothesis. It has, however, grown: the core comparison, a level-wise analysis and a two-point label-budget curve are now in one problem, which blurs which result is primary.
Clarity.feedback: Mark the mask-free versus mask-supervised comparison as primary and the level-wise analysis and label-budget points as secondary analyses.

Relevance.review: Unchanged and high: it addresses the verified mask dependence of MVFA's localisation (L3, L5, L18) and the unused image-labelled half of the benchmark.

Originality.review: The added hypothesis — that weak supervision through similarities to modality-shared text anchors gives localisation that transfers to an unseen modality, emerging mainly at deeper levels — turns a known technique (MIL) into a specific, testable claim about this architecture that the related work ([22], [29], [40], [58]) does not address.
Originality.feedback: To strengthen the claim, include a control in which the text anchors are replaced by a learned linear head, so that the role of the text anchors is isolated.

Feasibility.review: Still a one-term change at the original compute, with a sensible collapse check. The two label-budget variants add two more trainings per fold and seed, roughly tripling the training cost; on one GPU over a few weeks this is manageable but tight with 3 seeds.
Feasibility.feedback: Run the label-budget variants with one seed on two folds if time is short.

Significance.review: If confirmed, MVFA-style adaptation becomes trainable from report-level labels on all five source datasets; the label-budget curve makes the result directly usable for annotation planning.

versions.problem: In MVFA's zero-shot (leave-one-modality-out) training, the segmentation adapters — the only part that produces anomaly maps — are trained with Dice and Focal losses exclusively on the three source datasets that have pixel masks (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC), while OCT17, ChestXray and HIS only train the detection adapters. Primary question: can the segmentation adapters be trained from image-level labels alone, and how much mask-supervised localisation does that retain on the unseen modality? Primary outcomes: pixel-level AUROC and AUPRO on the held-out folds with masks (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC) and image-level AUROC on all folds, mask-supervised versus image-label-supervised MVFA under the shared protocol. Secondary analyses: (i) a control in which the text anchors of the segmentation branch are replaced by a learned linear patch classifier trained with the same MIL loss, isolating the role of the text anchors; (ii) a per-level breakdown; (iii) two label-budget points with masks for 10% and 25% of the abnormal source images (one seed, two folds).

Image-level labels are cheap and available for every BMAD dataset, yet MVFA never uses them to supervise where anomalies are. The related literature does not answer whether text-anchored patch similarities inside a multi-level CLIP adapter can learn transferable localisation from weak labels: MedSAD-CLIP [40] and MLCA [58] keep pixel-level supervision, MadCLIP [29] and the consistency-margin adapter [54] rely on labelled abnormal images, MediCLIP [22], AnomaMed [53] and the UWF framework [43] replace labels with synthetic anomalies, and image-level supervision has been used for separate generative models [10] rather than for the adapter's own maps. The text-anchor control turns the transfer hypothesis into a falsifiable claim about this architecture. The change is one loss term in the public training script at the original compute budget, with a one-fold pilot that checks for collapsed maps; success makes MVFA trainable from report-level labels, and failure, with the label-budget points, quantifies what masks are worth for cross-modality localisation — the annotation cost that L18 says is never measured.

Clarity.review: The primary question, primary outcomes and the three secondary analyses are now clearly separated, and every design choice is specified. The problem statement is long, and three secondary analyses stretch the 'one well-delimited question' requirement, although the primary comparison is unambiguous.
Clarity.feedback: Consider moving the per-level breakdown into the rationale or the evaluation plan to keep the problem statement focused.

Relevance.review: High and unchanged: verified mask dependence of localisation (L3, L5, L18) and the unused image-labelled half of the benchmark.

Originality.review: The text-anchor control makes the hypothesis falsifiable and specific to MVFA's architecture; the combination of MIL supervision of text-anchored multi-level maps with an unseen-modality test is not covered by [22], [29], [40], [54] or [58].

Feasibility.review: The primary comparison costs the same as MVFA's own training; the text-anchor control adds one training per fold and seed, and the label-budget points are restricted to one seed and two folds. Manageable on one GPU in a few weeks, with the collapse pilot as a sensible first step.
Feasibility.feedback: Prioritise the primary comparison and the text-anchor control; drop the label-budget points if time runs short.

Significance.review: Removing the need for dense masks from MVFA's source training would make the method trainable from report-level labels; the result is useful either way.

versions.problem: MVFA's image-level anomaly score is formed by different pooling rules in different places: the paper's image-level loss (Eq. 3) uses the maximum over the anomaly map, the released code trains the detection adapters with a mean-pooled map, and at inference the image score on datasets with masks is the maximum of the fused pixel map while on datasets without masks it is the mean-pooled detection score. Which image-level pooling of the fused anomaly map — maximum, mean, or top-k mean with k as a fraction of the image area in {0.1%, 1%, 5%} — gives the best and most stable few-shot and zero-shot image-level AUROC on each BMAD dataset, and how sensitive is each rule to isolated false-positive pixels, measured by the drop in image-level AUROC when a single high-scoring spurious patch is injected into the maps of normal test images? Training stays as in the released code; only the inference-time pooling changes, and the same rule is applied to all six datasets.
versions.rationale: L38 and C3 show that one spurious patch can decide an image's label and that the paper and the code disagree on pooling, while L30 shows that the scoring pipeline differs between datasets, so the reported detection numbers cannot be attributed to the method as described. The related literature varies the scoring head but does not isolate pooling for medical CLIP adapters: PatchCore [15] and WinCLIP [12] use maxima, HeadCLIP [17] and LaRP-CLIP [57] add joint or prototype image scores, and CANOR [30] argues that uniform max or mean aggregation of per-class scores ignores how findings combine in chest X-rays. Medical anomalies range from tiny lesions (BrainMRI, LiverCT) to diffuse changes (ChestXray, HIS), so the best pooling rule plausibly depends on the modality, which makes the question relevant to generalisation. It is inference-only on retrained checkpoints, needs a few lines in the test scripts, and yields a single documented scoring rule plus a robustness measure that complements AUROC (L8).

Clarity.review: The candidate pooling rules and the robustness test are clear, but 'the fused anomaly map' is ambiguous for the three datasets without masks, where the released code scores images from the detection map; the magnitude and size of the injected spurious patch are not defined; and 'most stable' is not operationalised.
Clarity.feedback: Name the map that is pooled on each dataset, define the injected patch (e.g., one patch set to the 99.9th percentile of abnormal-image scores) and define stability as the standard deviation over seeds and support draws.

Relevance.review: Addresses L38, C3 and L30 directly: the disagreement between paper and code on pooling and the dataset-dependent scoring make the reported detection numbers hard to attribute.
Relevance.feedback: Connect the result to B-group calibration: the pooling rule changes score distributions and therefore any threshold.

Originality.review: Comparing max, mean and top-k pooling is a routine ablation in anomaly detection ([12], [15]); the injected-patch robustness test is a small addition. The question is useful for reproducibility but has little novelty.
Originality.feedback: Add a hypothesis that goes beyond the ablation, e.g., that the optimal k scales with the typical lesion area of each modality and can be set from source modalities alone.

Feasibility.review: Trivially feasible: a few lines in the test scripts, inference on retrained checkpoints, no new training.

Significance.review: A documented, consistent scoring rule improves reproducibility, but the expected gains in AUROC are small and the result is unlikely to change how the field approaches medical anomaly detection.
Significance.feedback: Raise significance by linking the choice of k to modality properties that would let a practitioner set it for a new modality.

versions.problem: MVFA's image score uses different pooling rules in different places — the paper's Eq. 3 takes the maximum over the anomaly map, the released code trains the detection adapters with a mean-pooled map, and inference scores masked datasets by the maximum of the fused segmentation map and unmasked datasets by the mean-pooled detection map. Is the best image-level pooling of the fused segmentation map a function of the typical lesion area of a modality, so that it can be chosen for an unseen modality from the source modalities alone? Candidates: maximum, mean, and top-k mean with k in {0.1%, 1%, 5%, 20%} of the patches, applied to the fused segmentation map on all six datasets. The k chosen on the source modalities' validation split (shared protocol) is compared with the best k in hindsight and with the code's dataset-dependent rule, by image-level AUROC (mean and standard deviation over seeds and support draws) in the zero-shot and few-shot settings. Robustness: the drop in image-level AUROC when one patch of each normal test map is set to the 99.9th percentile of abnormal-image patch scores.
versions.rationale: L38 and C3 show that one spurious patch can decide an image's label and that the paper and the code disagree on pooling; L30 shows that the scoring pipeline differs between datasets, so the reported detection numbers cannot be attributed to the method as described. Pooling ablations exist in industrial anomaly detection ([12], [15]), and medical CLIP methods add joint or prototype image scores ([17], [57]); CANOR [30] argues that uniform max or mean aggregation ignores how chest X-ray findings combine. What is not known is whether the right pooling transfers across medical modalities whose anomalies range from small focal lesions (BrainMRI, LiverCT) to diffuse changes (ChestXray, HIS). The study is inference-only on retrained checkpoints and needs a few lines in the test scripts; it yields one documented rule and a selection procedure a practitioner can apply to a new modality.

Clarity.review: The map being pooled, the k grid, the selection rule and the robustness test are now defined. The central hypothesis relies on the 'typical lesion area' of a modality, which cannot be measured on the three datasets without masks, so the claimed relation cannot be tested on half of the benchmark.
Clarity.feedback: State how lesion area is estimated where masks are absent, or restrict the hypothesis test to the masked datasets.

Relevance.review: Addresses L38, C3 and L30; the selection-from-source-modalities framing ties it to the generalisation claim of the target paper.

Originality.review: Selecting the pooling rule from source modalities and relating it to lesion size goes a little beyond a routine ablation ([12], [15]), but remains a modest extension.

Significance.review: A consistent, transferable pooling rule improves reproducibility; the effect on detection AUROC is likely small.

Can one image-level pooling rule for the fused segmentation map be selected on the source modalities and transferred to the unseen one? Candidates: maximum, mean, and top-k mean with k in {0.1%, 1%, 5%, 20%} of the patches, applied to the fused segmentation map on all six datasets; k is chosen on the source modalities' validation split (shared protocol) and compared with the best k in hindsight and with the code's dataset-dependent rule, by image-level AUROC (mean and standard deviation over seeds and support draws) in the zero-shot and few-shot settings. Robustness: the drop in image-level AUROC when one patch of each normal test map is set to the 99.9th percentile of abnormal-image patch scores. Secondary hypothesis, tested on the three datasets with masks only: the best k increases with the median lesion area.

Clarity.review: The transfer question, the selection procedure and the robustness test are clear, and the lesion-area hypothesis is now restricted to the masked datasets.

Originality.review: A modest extension of a standard pooling ablation ([12], [15]) with a transfer-selection step.

Significance.review: Improves reproducibility of MVFA's detection numbers; expected AUROC effects are small.

versions.problem: In MVFA's few-shot mode, the released code defines a K-shot support set as K normal and K abnormal target-domain images, the abnormal ones loaded with expert pixel masks, and uses them both to fine-tune the adapters (Dice, Focal and BCE losses) and to fill the memory bank. Can the K real abnormal images with masks be replaced by synthetic abnormal images made from the K normal supports alone — lesion-like patches cut from other normal images of the same modality, intensity-perturbed and Poisson-blended into the support, with the pasted region as the free mask — and how much of the few-shot image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and AUPRO of real-abnormal MVFA does this normal-only variant keep on each BMAD dataset for K in {2, 4, 8, 16}? A memory-bank-only variant (no fine-tuning on target data) is reported as the lower reference.
versions.rationale: L4 and L18, confirmed in the released code, show that 'K = 4' means four normal plus four expertly delineated abnormal slices, the most expensive annotation in medical imaging, and the paper never measures what those abnormal images and masks contribute. Several related methods show that synthetic anomalies can stand in for real ones when adapting CLIP to medical images (MediCLIP [22], AnomaMed's anomaly blending [53], the UWF framework's Poisson blending [43], LesionPaste [32]), and [55] shows that selecting informative synthetic images matters; but none of them measures the gap to real abnormal supervision inside the same adapter, on the same support set, under an unseen-modality protocol. The question isolates one component — the abnormal half of MVFA's few-shot support set — keeps architecture, losses and evaluation unchanged, and needs only image operations on data that BMAD already provides, so it is feasible on one GPU; its answer tells a hospital whether MVFA's few-shot mode can be used before any abnormal case has been annotated.

Clarity.review: The component (the abnormal half of the K-shot support set), the replacement and the outcomes are stated, and the memory-bank-only lower reference is useful. The synthesis recipe is described loosely: patch size and shape, the intensity perturbation and how many synthetic images are made per support are not given, and it is unclear whether synthetic images also enter the memory bank.
Clarity.feedback: Fix the synthesis parameters (e.g., elliptical patches of 2-15% of the image area, one synthetic image per normal support and epoch) and state that the memory bank keeps only real normal supports.

Relevance.review: Directly addresses L4 and L18: the released code confirms that K-shot means K expertly masked abnormal images, the costliest annotation, and the paper never measures their contribution.
Relevance.feedback: Frame the outcome as the annotation cost that the synthetic variant removes per target site.

Originality.review: Synthetic anomalies for adapting CLIP to medical images are already common ([22], [32], [43], [53], [55]). The contribution is a controlled measurement — synthetic versus real abnormal supports inside the same adapter, with the same support set and protocol — which is useful but not a new method.
Originality.feedback: Sharpen the question with a hypothesis that the literature does not settle, e.g., that the gap depends on lesion size or modality (focal BrainMRI/LiverCT lesions versus diffuse ChestXray/HIS findings).

Feasibility.review: Only image operations on data BMAD already provides, the existing losses and the same training budget as the original few-shot runs; 4 K values x 6 datasets x 3 seeds x 3 draws is a sizeable but manageable grid on one GPU. Poisson blending needs care on single-channel images.
Feasibility.feedback: Reduce the grid if needed by running K in {2, 8} for all datasets and the full K range on two datasets.

Significance.review: Practically relevant for deployment at a new site, but the expected outcome — synthetic anomalies recover part of the gain — is close to what [22] and [55] already report, so the result is likely to be incremental unless the modality dependence is analysed.
Significance.feedback: Tie the result to a concrete decision rule (when real abnormal annotations are worth collecting).

versions.problem: In MVFA's few-shot mode, the released code defines a K-shot support set as K normal and K abnormal target-domain images, the abnormal ones with expert pixel masks, used to fine-tune the adapters (Dice, Focal and BCE losses), while the memory bank holds the normal supports. Can the K real abnormal images with masks be replaced by synthetic abnormal images built from the K normal supports alone, and does the size of the gap depend on the type of lesion? Synthesis: one synthetic image per normal support and epoch, made by Poisson-blending an elliptical patch (2-15% of the image area) cut from a different normal image of the same modality, with random intensity scaling, the pasted region serving as the mask; the memory bank keeps only real normal supports. Outcomes per BMAD dataset for K in {2, 8} (full range K in {2, 4, 8, 16} on BrainMRI and ChestXray): few-shot image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and AUPRO of the synthetic variant relative to real-abnormal MVFA, with a memory-bank-only variant as the lower reference. Hypothesis: the synthetic variant recovers most of the gain on focal-lesion datasets (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC) and little on diffuse-finding datasets (ChestXray, HIS, OCT17).
versions.rationale: L4 and L18, confirmed in the released code, show that 'K = 4' means four normal plus four expertly delineated abnormal slices, and the paper never measures what those abnormal images contribute. Synthetic anomalies are a known substitute when adapting CLIP to medical images (MediCLIP [22], LesionPaste [32], the UWF framework's Poisson blending [43], AnomaMed [53]), and [55] shows that the choice of synthetic images matters; but none measures the gap to real abnormal supervision inside the same adapter with the same support set, and none asks for which kinds of medical anomaly the substitution fails. The question isolates the abnormal half of the support set, keeps architecture, losses and evaluation unchanged, needs only image operations on BMAD data, and is sized to one GPU; its answer is a decision rule for a new site: when collecting K annotated abnormal cases is worth the expert time.

Clarity.review: The synthesis recipe, the memory-bank content, the K grid and the hypothesis are now explicit. Two questions remain bundled (can the abnormal supports be replaced, and does the gap depend on lesion type), and 'focal' versus 'diffuse' is asserted for each dataset rather than defined.
Clarity.feedback: Define the focal/diffuse grouping operationally (e.g., median lesion area from masks where available) or present it as a post-hoc analysis.

Relevance.review: Addresses L4 and L18 directly; the decision-rule framing makes the deployment relevance explicit.

Originality.review: The lesion-type hypothesis adds a question the synthetic-anomaly literature ([22], [43], [53], [55]) leaves open, but the core manipulation remains a well-known substitution of real by synthetic anomalies.
Originality.feedback: Consider testing a property specific to MVFA, e.g., whether synthetic supports harm the zero-shot text branch through the shared adapters.

Feasibility.review: The reduced grid fits one GPU; synthesis is cheap; all losses and scripts exist.

Significance.review: A decision rule about when annotated abnormal cases are worth collecting is useful for practice, and a dataset-dependent answer would be informative; still, the expected result is partly anticipated by [22] and [55].
Significance.feedback: Report the annotation time saved per site alongside the AUROC gap.
